summary:
Guadeloupe stands under France's national framework: French criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute, the marriage regime and the rules on identity documents apply here as they do in the metropole. Same-sex relations were decriminalised in the Penal Code of 1791 and retained in the 1810 Code, though public morality provisions continued to be used against LGBTQ people. Same-sex marriage is available, gender-identity discrimination is prohibited, and no legal penalty attaches to trans existence.

Legal gender recognition has followed the simplified French procedure since 1 January 2017 under a law signed on 18 November 2016. Surgery and medical diagnosis are no longer required, and self-certification of gender and proof of medical treatment were dropped from the final bill. A change of first name can be handled at the registry office, while a change of the gender marker still requires an appearance before a court. A 2017 bid to have the law recognise a 'neutral sex' classification was rejected by the Court of Cassation, and in 2022 a court of appeal ruled that a transgender woman should be regarded as the mother of a child she conceived before her sex change.

Discriminatory and violent conduct is prosecuted under the law of 31 December 2004, which made homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic comments criminal, with a maximum penalty of a €45,000 fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment, and amended the 1881 Freedom of the Press Law to cover injury, defamation, insult and incitement to hatred, violence or discrimination on grounds of gender, sexual orientation or disability. Christian Vanneste, a serving MP, became the first person convicted under it in January 2006, though the Court of Cassation later cancelled that conviction. A conversion therapy ban passed the Senate on 7 December 2020 and was published on 1 February 2022, carrying two years' imprisonment and/or a €30,000 fine.

Reported homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults rose 36% in 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims against about 1,380 in 2018, a figure released on 16 May 2020. In October 2018 President Macron denounced homophobic violence as 'unworthy of France' after a rise in attacks.

Access to gender-affirming care is constrained in practice. A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found significant problems in that healthcare: lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access depending on location, recommending an informed-consent model. Gender dysphoria was declassified as a mental illness by decree in 2010, though French trans organisations said nothing changed beyond the announcement; transsexualism remains listed under ALD 31 with treatment funded by the Sécurité Sociale, and gender-affirming surgery has been legal domestically since 1979. The Académie Nationale de Médecine characterised the rise in trans people seeking treatment as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and 'a primarily social problem' and advised extreme caution on access, without changing practice.

Trans minors are a live legislative target. In March 2024 centre-right senators commissioned a report from the Little Mermaid Observatory, a body opposed to all gender transition for minors, which called transition a 'health scandal' and transness a 'social contagion'. A bill banning medical transition under 18 passed the Senate in May 2024, opposed by the Macron government, and prompted large-scale protests; no further update is recorded after 23 July 2024. In late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued the country's first trans youth guidelines, recommending puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2. In 2022 it emerged that the president of the scientific committee of DILCRAH, France's interministerial body against racism, anti-Semitism and anti-LGBT hatred, sat on the Little Mermaid Observatory; one member resigned and the president stepped away.

Custodial settings are the documented risk area. A BuzzFeed News report of January 2018 found that in French prisons, whose rules govern detention in Guadeloupe, the placement of trans women follows the legal gender recorded on the incarceration papers, which may not correspond to the person's presentation; in practice assignment is said to weigh the individual's best interests, with individual cells or placement in more welcoming wings used where possible. The national preventive mechanism (CGLPL) issued an opinion on 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty, finding that serious violations of fundamental rights persist across places of detention, drawing on some 40 referrals since 2010.

Practical support exists on the island. Guadeloupe's first LGBT+ centre, the Maison des Diversités et de l'Inclusion, opened on 24 April 2024, offering reception, support and orientation for people of diverse identity, sexual, bodily and gender diversities, driven by a federation of Guadeloupean associations; the opening was attended by the visiting national minister Aurore Bergé, who announced measures to strengthen the fight against gender-based violence and discrimination in Guadeloupe, with structures adapted for overseas territories. Community organisations including Secret's Out, Queer Gang and Lovo Nova partnered on a year of LGBT-friendly social events across Guadeloupe in 2025, and activists interviewed in September 2023 described reconciliation of community life with local identity and organising advancing after sister island Martinique.

In education, the national Ministry of Education launched the campaign 'Tous égaux, tous alliés' in January 2019 to tackle anti-LGBTQ bullying, providing reporting services, a helpline and guidance requirements, with 17 May as a sensitisation day. In March 2019 the Higher Education Minister announced that all higher education institutions should use transgender people's preferred names, including on student cards and exam forms.
tangentialFactors:
The legislative direction at the national level is unsettled rather than settled in one direction. The Senate's May 2024 passage of a ban on medical transition under 18 sits alongside the late-2024 paediatric endocrinology guidelines recommending puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2, so a visitor with dependants should expect contested rules rather than a single operative standard.

Official bodies have been shown to overlap with advocacy opposed to transition. The 2022 disclosure that DILCRAH's scientific committee president sat on the Little Mermaid Observatory produced one resignation and the president's departure, which bears on how much weight to give statements from that machinery.

Parental recognition has moved in a permissive direction: the Court of Cassation ruled on 5 July 2017 that a child born to a surrogate abroad can be adopted by the partner of the biological father, the Court of Appeal of Paris held in May 2019 that a Canadian birth certificate must be recognised, and in December 2019 the Court of Cassation ruled that foreign birth certificates recognising same-sex partners must be fully recognised in France.

Historical context shapes the enforcement culture: the Vichy-era consent differential of 21 for homosexual relations against 15 for heterosexual relations, in force from 6 August 1942 and equalised only on 4 August 1982, and the Mirguet amendment of 1960 doubling penalties for indecent exposure in homosexual activity until its 1980 repeal, both left a public morality apparatus that outlived decriminalisation. A compensation bill for men arrested under article 330 before 1980 passed the National Assembly unanimously in March 2024 and awaits a Senate vote.

Organising capacity is described as following Martinique, so developments on that neighbouring island are a reasonable early indicator of what reaches Guadeloupe.
localsOnly:
Residents seeking a legal gender change use the two-step route available since 2017: the first name is changed at the registry office, and the gender marker is changed by application to a court, with no surgery or medical diagnosis required and no self-certification or proof of treatment demanded.

Residents with long-term treatment needs are covered under ALD 31, which funds transsexualism-related care through the Sécurité Sociale, and gender-affirming surgery has been legal in France since 1979. In practice, ILGA-Europe's 2022 findings on waiting times and location-dependent access apply to residents as much as to visitors.

Local association life is anchored by the Maison des Diversités et de l'Inclusion, run by a federation of Guadeloupean associations since 24 April 2024, and by groups including Secret's Out, Queer Gang, Lovo Nova and Amalgame Humani's, which organised a year of social events across Guadeloupe in 2025.

Residents benefit from the national education measures: the 'Tous égaux, tous alliés' campaign of January 2019 with its reporting services and helpline, the 17 May sensitisation day, and the March 2019 instruction that higher education institutions use transgender people's preferred names on student cards and exam forms.

Discriminatory conduct by residents or officials is covered by the law of 31 December 2004 and by the conversion therapy ban in force since 1 February 2022, and residents may report to the CGLPL, whose 25 May 2021 opinion covers places of deprivation of liberty in Guadeloupe.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Guadeloupe-specific enforcement data is sourced. The 36% rise in attacks and the 1,870 figure are national police counts for 2019, and the inventory contains no breakdown for Guadeloupe, so the local incidence of anti-trans violence is unresolved.

The status of the Senate's May 2024 bill banning medical transition under 18 after 23 July 2024 is unresolved in the sources; whether it was withdrawn, amended or advanced is not sourced here.

Whether trans detainees have in practice been placed according to legal gender in Guadeloupe's own detention facilities is not sourced. The BuzzFeed News account describes the French prison system generally, and the CGLPL opinion is framed nationally, so the local application is inferred from the governing rules rather than documented.

The availability of gender-affirming care providers within Guadeloupe itself is not sourced. ILGA-Europe's 2022 findings on inequitable access by location are national in scope and do not identify which services, if any, are present on the island.

Whether the Maison des Diversités et de l'Inclusion offers trans-specific services, as distinct from general reception and orientation, is not stated in the sources.
